content: Pim-1, also known as proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase Pim-1, is an enzyme encoded by the PIM1 gene in humans. It is classified as a proto-oncogene and encodes a serine/threonine kinase of the same name. The oncogenic role of Pim-1 was first identified in murine T-cell lymphomas, where it was frequently activated by the Moloney murine leukemia virus. Since then, Pim-1 has been implicated in various human cancers, including prostate cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, and other hematopoietic malignancies. Pim-1 is predominantly expressed in tissues such as the spleen, thymus, bone marrow, prostate, oral epithelium, hippocampus, and fetal liver. Additionally, it is highly expressed in tumor-derived cell cultures. Functionally, Pim-1 is involved in regulating cell cycle progression, apoptosis, transcriptional activation, and broader signal transduction pathways. The PIM1 gene is located on chromosome 6 (6p21.2) and spans approximately 5 kilobases of DNA, comprising six exons and five introns. Its expression is regulated by the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, with transcription factors STAT3 and STAT5 directly binding to the Pim-1 promoter to initiate transcription. The gene is evolutionarily conserved across species, including dogs, cows, mice, rats, zebrafish, and C. elegans. Interestingly, mice deficient in Pim-1 exhibit no overt phenotypic abnormalities, suggesting functional redundancy with other kinases. Indeed, two other kinases, Pim-2 and Pim-3, share structural and functional similarities with Pim-1. The PIM1 gene produces two protein isoforms, 34 kDa and 44 kDa, due to alternative translation initiation sites. The Pim-1 protein consists of 313 amino acids and exhibits a high degree of conservation across species, with 94–97% amino acid identity between human, murine, and rat Pim-1. The active site of Pim-1, spanning amino acids 38–290, contains conserved motifs such as a glycine loop, a phosphate-binding site, and a proton acceptor site. A single amino acid substitution at position 67 (lysine to methionine) results in the inactivation of the kinase. Pim-1 is primarily activated in response to cytokine signaling and is involved in numerous signal transduction pathways. Its transcription is regulated by STAT3 and STAT5, which are themselves activated by cytokines such as interleukins (IL-2, IL-3, IL-5, IL-6, IL-7, IL-12, IL-15), prolactin, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα), epidermal growth factor (EGF), and interferon-gamma (IFNγ). Pim-1 can also bind to negative regulators of the JAK/STAT pathway, creating a negative feedback loop. Although the post-transcriptional modifications of Pim-1 are not well understood, it is hypothesized that heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) plays a role in its folding and stabilization. Additionally, the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2 has been implicated in Pim-1 degradation. Pim-1 interacts with a variety of proteins, including CBX3, CDC25A, Hsp90 (cytosolic member A1), NFATC1, nuclear mitotic apparatus protein 1, p21, SND1, and RELA. Other substrates and binding partners include proteins involved in transcription regulation, such as nuclear adaptor protein p100, HP-1, PAP-1, TRAF2/SNX6, and regulators of the JAK/STAT pathway, such as SOCS1 and SOCS3. Pim-1 also acts as a cofactor for the transcription factor c-Myc, which regulates approximately 15% of all genes. The synergy between Pim-1 and c-Myc has been implicated in prostate tumorigenesis. Pim-1 is capable of phosphorylating numerous targets, including itself, many of which are involved in cell cycle regulation. Pim-1 activates several key proteins, including: Cdc25C (G1/S positive regulator): Activation promotes the G1 to S phase transition. Cdc25C (G2/M positive regulator): Activation promotes the G2 to M phase transition. Pim-1 deactivates several proteins, including: Bad (pro-apoptotic protein): Deactivation enhances cell survival. CKI (G1/S negative regulator): Deactivation promotes the G1 to S phase transition. C-TAK1 (Cdc25C inhibitor): Deactivation promotes the G2 to M phase transition. Clinically, Pim-1 plays a critical role in regulating cell cycle progression and apoptosis and has been implicated in various cancers, including prostate cancer, Burkitt’s lymphoma, oral cancer, and hematopoietic lymphomas. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the PIM1 gene have been associated with an increased risk of lung cancer in Korean populations and have also been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphomas. Beyond its role in cancer, Pim-1 has been suggested as a potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer’s disease. Notably, Pim-1 expression has been linked to resistance against anti-angiogenic therapies in prostate and colon cancer models, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Numerous small-molecule inhibitors targeting Pim-1 have been developed, with some showing promising anti-cancer activity in clinical trials. However, challenges such as insufficient selectivity and associated side effects have limited their clinical utility. Research efforts are ongoing to develop more potent and selective Pim-1 inhibitors. Examples of Pim-1 inhibitors include: AZD1208 LGH447 SGI-1776 TP-3654
